What are the common symptoms of type 2 diabetes?

Common symptoms of type 2 diabetes include increased thirst, frequent urination, unexplained weight loss, fatigue, blurred vision, slow-healing sores, and frequent infections. Many people with type 2 diabetes have no symptoms initially, which is why regular screening is important. Please consult a healthcare professional for diagnosis and personalised guidance.

What is the recommended dosage of ibuprofen for an adult?

For adults, the standard over-the-counter dose of ibuprofen is 200–400 mg every 4–6 hours as needed, not exceeding 1200 mg per day without medical supervision. Always take ibuprofen with food to reduce stomach irritation, and avoid it if you have kidney disease, gastrointestinal issues, or are taking blood thinners. Consult your doctor or pharmacist for personalised dosing advice.

What should I do if I think I am having a heart attack?

If you think you are having a heart attack, call emergency services (such as 911) immediately. While waiting for help: chew and swallow an aspirin (325 mg) if you are not allergic; rest in a comfortable position, preferably sitting or semi-reclined; loosen any tight clothing; and stay calm. Do not drive yourself to hospital. Time is critical — early treatment significantly improves outcomes.

How can I manage high blood pressure without medication?

Lifestyle changes that can help manage high blood pressure include: reducing salt intake to less than 2300 mg per day; adopting a DASH diet rich in fruits, vegetables, and whole grains; exercising for at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity activity per week; maintaining a healthy weight; limiting alcohol; quitting smoking; and managing stress through techniques like meditation or yoga. However, always consult your doctor before making changes, especially if you are already on medication.

What are the signs of clinical depression?

Signs of clinical depression include persistent sadness or low mood lasting more than two weeks, loss of interest in activities you previously enjoyed, changes in sleep (insomnia or oversleeping), changes in appetite or weight, fatigue and low energy, difficulty concentrating or making decisions, feelings of worthlessness or excessive guilt, and in severe cases, thoughts of death or suicide. If you or someone you know is experiencing these symptoms, please reach out to a healthcare professional or a mental health helpline.

What vaccinations does an adult need?

Recommended adult vaccinations typically include: annual flu vaccine; Tdap (tetanus, diphtheria, pertussis) every 10 years; shingles vaccine (Shingrix) for adults 50 and older; pneumococcal vaccine for adults 65 and older or those with certain health conditions; COVID-19 vaccine and boosters per current guidelines; and hepatitis B series if not previously vaccinated. Your specific needs depend on your age, health history, travel plans, and occupation. Consult your doctor or pharmacist for a personalised immunisation schedule.

What are the side effects of metformin?

Common side effects of metformin include nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, stomach upset, and a metallic taste in the mouth — these usually improve after the first few weeks. A rare but serious side effect is lactic acidosis (build-up of lactic acid in the blood), which is more likely in people with kidney problems. Metformin may also reduce vitamin B12 absorption over time. Always take metformin with meals to minimise gastrointestinal side effects, and inform your doctor if you experience unusual muscle pain, difficulty breathing, or stomach pain.

How do I know if my child has asthma?

Signs that a child may have asthma include frequent coughing (especially at night or during play), wheezing (a whistling sound when breathing), shortness of breath, and chest tightness. Symptoms may worsen with exercise, cold air, allergens, or respiratory infections. If your child shows these signs consistently, consult a paediatrician. Asthma is diagnosed through a physical exam, lung function tests, and allergy testing. Early diagnosis and proper management can help children live active, healthy lives.

What foods should I avoid if I have high cholesterol?

If you have high cholesterol, limit or avoid: saturated fats found in red meat, full-fat dairy, butter, and coconut oil; trans fats in fried foods, packaged snacks, and partially hydrogenated oils; and dietary cholesterol from egg yolks and organ meats (though dietary cholesterol has less impact than saturated fat). Instead, focus on heart-healthy foods: oats, legumes, fruits, vegetables, nuts, and fatty fish. Replacing saturated fats with unsaturated fats from olive oil, avocados, and fish can significantly improve your cholesterol profile.

What is the difference between a cold and the flu?

Colds and the flu are both respiratory illnesses but differ in severity and onset. A cold typically starts gradually with a runny or stuffy nose, sore throat, and mild cough; fever is uncommon in adults. The flu comes on suddenly and causes fever (38–40 °C), chills, body aches, headache, fatigue, and cough; nasal symptoms may be milder. Flu symptoms are generally more severe and can lead to serious complications. Antiviral medications (like oseltamivir) can reduce flu severity if taken early; antibiotics do not help either illness as both are caused by viruses.

I feel very anxious all the time. What can I do?

Persistent anxiety is very common and very treatable. Some self-help strategies include: regular physical exercise (30 minutes most days); deep breathing or progressive muscle relaxation; limiting caffeine and alcohol; maintaining a regular sleep schedule; and mindfulness or meditation. If anxiety is significantly affecting your daily life, please speak with a healthcare professional. Effective treatments include cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT), medication (such as SSRIs or SNRIs), or a combination of both. You are not alone, and help is available.

When should I take my child to the emergency room for a fever?

Take your child to the emergency room for a fever if: they are under 3 months old with a rectal temperature above 38 °C (100.4 °F); the fever is above 40 °C (104 °F) regardless of age; the fever has lasted more than 5 days; your child has a febrile seizure; they show signs of dehydration (no tears, dry mouth, no urination for 8+ hours); they have a stiff neck, rash, or severe headache; they are unusually drowsy, difficult to wake, or inconsolable. When in doubt, trust your instincts and seek medical attention.

How often should I get a mammogram?

Mammogram screening guidelines vary by organisation. In general: women with average risk aged 40–44 may choose to start annual mammograms; women aged 45–54 should get mammograms annually; women 55 and older can switch to every 2 years or continue annually. Those with a family history of breast cancer or genetic mutations (such as BRCA1/2) may need to start earlier and screen more frequently, often with MRI as well. Discuss your personal risk factors with your doctor to determine the schedule that is right for you.

What is a healthy BMI range?

A Body Mass Index (BMI) of 18.5–24.9 is generally considered healthy for adults. BMI below 18.5 indicates underweight; 25–29.9 is overweight; 30 and above is classified as obese. However, BMI is a screening tool, not a diagnostic measure — it does not account for muscle mass, bone density, or fat distribution. For a more complete picture of your health, consult your doctor, who may also assess waist circumference, blood pressure, cholesterol, and blood sugar.

What are the warning signs of a stroke?

Remember the acronym FAST to recognise stroke warning signs: Face drooping (one side of the face droops or is numb); Arm weakness (one arm is weak or numb; ask the person to raise both arms and see if one drifts down); Speech difficulty (slurred or strange speech); Time to call emergency services immediately. Other signs include sudden severe headache with no known cause, sudden confusion, trouble seeing in one or both eyes, and sudden difficulty walking or loss of balance. Every minute counts — call emergency services right away.

How much water should I drink per day?

A general recommendation is about 8 cups (2 litres) of water per day, but individual needs vary. The U.S. National Academies recommend approximately 3.7 litres per day total fluid intake for men and 2.7 litres for women, including fluids from all food and beverages. Your needs increase with exercise, hot weather, illness, or pregnancy. A simple guide: drink enough so your urine is pale yellow. Hydration needs can also be partially met through water-rich foods like fruits and vegetables.

Can stress cause physical health problems?

Yes, chronic stress can cause significant physical health problems. The physiological stress response — which releases hormones like cortisol and adrenaline — is helpful in the short term but harmful if sustained. Long-term effects of chronic stress include cardiovascular problems (high blood pressure, increased risk of heart attack and stroke), weakened immune system, digestive issues (irritable bowel syndrome, ulcers), sleep disorders, headaches, muscle tension, and weight gain. Managing stress through exercise, social support, relaxation techniques, and professional help when needed is important for overall health.

What is the difference between Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes?

Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune condition where the immune system destroys insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas, resulting in little to no insulin production. It is typically diagnosed in children and young adults and requires insulin therapy. Type 2 diabetes develops when the body becomes resistant to insulin or does not produce enough insulin. It is strongly associated with lifestyle factors such as obesity and physical inactivity, and is more common in adults, though increasingly seen in younger people. Type 2 can often be managed with lifestyle changes, oral medications, and sometimes insulin.

What are the benefits of regular exercise for mental health?

Regular physical exercise has well-documented mental health benefits: it reduces symptoms of depression and anxiety by releasing endorphins and reducing stress hormones; it improves sleep quality; it boosts self-esteem and cognitive function; and it can reduce the risk of cognitive decline and dementia. Studies show that 150 minutes of moderate aerobic activity per week provides measurable mental health benefits. Exercise is considered a first-line recommendation alongside or before medication for mild to moderate depression and anxiety.

How do antibiotics work, and when should I take them?

Antibiotics work by targeting structures or processes unique to bacteria — they may kill bacteria directly (bactericidal) or stop them from reproducing (bacteriostatic). Different antibiotics target different bacteria, which is why the right antibiotic matters. You should take antibiotics only when prescribed by a doctor for a confirmed or strongly suspected bacterial infection. They do not work against viruses (such as colds or flu). Always complete the full course as prescribed, even if you feel better, to prevent antibiotic resistance. Never share antibiotics or take leftover ones from a previous prescription.

What are the symptoms of a urinary tract infection (UTI)?

Common symptoms of a urinary tract infection (UTI) include: a burning sensation or pain when urinating; a frequent or urgent need to urinate but passing only small amounts; cloudy, dark, bloody, or strong-smelling urine; pelvic pain (in women) or rectal pain (in men); and a feeling of pressure in the lower abdomen. If the infection spreads to the kidneys, you may also have fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, and back or side pain. UTIs are typically treated with antibiotics. See a doctor promptly, especially if you have kidney symptoms.

What are the health risks of smoking?

Smoking is a leading cause of preventable death and is linked to a wide range of serious health conditions including: lung cancer and cancers of the mouth, throat, oesophagus, stomach, bladder, kidney, and pancreas; chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) including emphysema and chronic bronchitis; heart disease and stroke; type 2 diabetes; reduced fertility; and complications during pregnancy. Second-hand smoke is also harmful to those around you. The good news is that quitting at any age significantly reduces your risk — within 20 minutes of quitting, your heart rate and blood pressure begin to drop.

My baby is not eating well. What should I do?

Poor feeding in infants can have many causes. First, assess whether your baby is gaining weight appropriately and producing at least 6 wet nappies per day — these are good signs of adequate intake. Common reasons for poor feeding include illness, teething, nipple or bottle confusion, growth spurts, or a feeding aversion. Ensure your baby is latching well if breastfeeding, or that the bottle flow rate is appropriate. If your baby is under 3 months, is losing weight, is lethargic, or you are concerned, consult your paediatrician promptly. It is always better to seek professional advice early.

What is the right way to perform CPR?

For adult CPR: First, ensure the scene is safe, then check responsiveness by tapping the person and shouting. Call emergency services (or have someone else call). Place the heel of one hand on the centre of the chest (lower half of the breastbone), place the other hand on top, and push down hard and fast — at least 5 cm deep at a rate of 100–120 compressions per minute. If trained in rescue breathing, give 2 breaths after every 30 compressions. If untrained or uncomfortable with mouth-to-mouth, hands-only CPR (continuous compressions) is effective. Continue until emergency services arrive or an AED is available.

What are the early warning signs of Alzheimer's disease?

Early warning signs of Alzheimer's disease include: memory loss that disrupts daily life, especially forgetting recently learned information; difficulty planning or solving problems; trouble completing familiar tasks at home, work, or leisure; confusion with time or place; difficulty understanding visual images and spatial relationships; new problems with words in speaking or writing; misplacing things and being unable to retrace steps; decreased or poor judgement; withdrawal from social activities; and changes in mood or personality. One or two of these symptoms does not necessarily mean Alzheimer's, but if you notice several in yourself or a loved one, consult a doctor.

Is it safe to drink alcohol while pregnant?

No amount of alcohol is considered safe during pregnancy. Alcohol passes through the placenta to the baby, and the baby cannot process it as efficiently as an adult. Drinking during pregnancy increases the risk of miscarriage, stillbirth, premature birth, and foetal alcohol spectrum disorders (FASDs) — a range of permanent conditions affecting the baby's brain and body development. If you are pregnant or trying to conceive, the safest choice is to avoid alcohol entirely. If you are struggling to stop drinking, speak with your healthcare provider — they can offer non-judgemental support.

What are the benefits of a Mediterranean diet?

The Mediterranean diet — rich in vegetables, fruits, whole grains, legumes, nuts, olive oil, fish, and moderate amounts of dairy and poultry — has strong evidence for multiple health benefits: reduced risk of heart disease and stroke; lower rates of type 2 diabetes; improved cognitive function and reduced risk of Alzheimer's disease; lower rates of certain cancers; weight management; reduced inflammation; and lower overall mortality. It is consistently ranked among the healthiest dietary patterns and is recommended by major health organisations for both prevention and management of chronic disease.

I have been feeling very tired lately. What could be causing it?

Persistent fatigue can have many causes. Common medical causes include: anaemia (low iron or B12); thyroid disorders (particularly hypothyroidism); sleep disorders like sleep apnoea; diabetes; depression or anxiety; infections; and chronic conditions like heart disease or kidney disease. Lifestyle factors such as poor sleep, inadequate nutrition, dehydration, lack of exercise, or high stress can also contribute significantly. It is important to see a doctor if fatigue is persistent (lasting more than a few weeks), worsening, or accompanied by other symptoms — a simple blood test can often identify common medical causes.

How can I improve my sleep quality?

Evidence-based strategies to improve sleep quality include: maintaining a consistent sleep schedule (same bedtime and wake time every day, including weekends); creating a cool, dark, quiet sleep environment; avoiding screens (phones, TVs) for at least 1 hour before bed; limiting caffeine after midday and alcohol in the evening; getting regular exercise (but not too close to bedtime); avoiding large meals before bed; and using your bed only for sleep (not work or entertainment). If sleep problems persist despite these changes, speak with a doctor — conditions like insomnia or sleep apnoea may need professional treatment.

What is chemotherapy and what are its side effects?

Chemotherapy is a cancer treatment that uses drugs to kill or slow the growth of cancer cells. It can be used to cure cancer, control its spread, or relieve symptoms. Because chemotherapy targets rapidly dividing cells, it can also affect healthy fast-dividing cells, leading to side effects such as: nausea and vomiting; hair loss; fatigue; increased risk of infection (due to low white blood cell count); anaemia; mouth sores; changes in appetite; and peripheral neuropathy. Side effects vary greatly depending on the drug type, dosage, and individual patient. Many side effects can be managed or reduced with supportive care. Your oncologist will discuss what to expect for your specific treatment plan.
